summary: Defines new SNMP MIB objects for managing connections when TCP and UDP run over IPX, in place of the usual connection and listener tables. It accompanies the TCP/UDP over IPX experiment and is itself experimental.

eli5.summary: A scoreboard for network helpers that keeps track of who is talking to whom, built for the special case where Internet messages ride on IPX.

questions: mib objects for tcp over ipx
how does snmp manage tcp connections
why use mib tables for ipx instead of ip
subtitle: SNMP management objects for TCP and UDP running over IPX instead of IP.

tldr.problem: When TCP and UDP run over IPX (a Novell network protocol) instead of IP, the standard SNMP MIB objects for managing connections do not work because they expect IP addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1792 defines new SNMP MIB tables (tcpIpxConnTable, udpIpxTable, and unspecified-network variants) that use IPX addresses instead of IP addresses to track active connections and listeners.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators using TCP/UDP over IPX can now monitor and manage connections with SNMP, using the same monitoring concepts they use for IP-based connections.

today: RFC 1792 remains an Experimental protocol and has not been updated or obsoleted. It defined SNMP management for TCP and UDP over IPX during the period when IPX networks existed alongside IP networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Traditionally, TCP and UDP run over the Internet Protocol (IP). Standard SNMP management defines objects to track these connections in RFC 1213. However, when TCP and UDP run over the Novell IPX protocol instead, those standard objects fail because they specify addresses as IP addresses, not IPX addresses.

This RFC defines new SNMP MIB objects designed for TCP and UDP running over IPX. These new tables replace the standard tcpConnTable and udpListenerTable when the network layer is IPX instead of IP, allowing network administrators to monitor these connections with the same SNMP tools.
sections.eli5: Imagine you have a directory of phone calls. If everyone uses phone numbers, one format works fine. But if some people use a different address system, you need a different directory.

sections.title: IPX Addresses
sections.content:
An IPX address consists of 10 octets (bytes): the first 4 octets represent a network number and the last 6 octets represent a node number (the physical address of a device). In text form, IPX addresses are written as hexadecimal digits separated by a colon: nnnnnnnn:mmmmmmmmmmmm.

This addressing scheme is fundamental to the new MIB objects, which use the IPX address type instead of the IP address type for identifying the source and destination of each connection or listener.
sections.eli5: An IPX address is like a complete mailing address: a network location (where the building is) and a node location (which mailbox in the building).

sections.title: TCP/IPX Connection Table
sections.content:
The TCP/IPX connection table (tcpIpxConnTable) stores information about each active TCP connection over IPX. Each entry in the table is indexed by four values: the local IPX address, the local port number, the remote IPX address, and the remote port number. This forms a unique key for every distinct connection.

Each connection entry records the current state of the TCP connection (closed, listen, established, closing, etc.), using the same 12-state model from RFC 793. A special state value allows a management station to delete the connection by setting the state to deleteTCB, which terminates the connection immediately.
sections.eli5: Each row in the table describes one conversation: who it is between (both sides and port numbers), and whether the conversation is just starting, fully open, or ending.

sections.title: UDP and Unspecified Network Tables
sections.content:
The UDP/IPX table (udpIpxTable) tracks UDP listeners over IPX. Unlike TCP connections, UDP endpoints are stateless, so the table records only the local IPX address and local port number for each listener application.

For cases where the network layer is not fully specified (such as listen sockets willing to accept connections on any IPX interface), RFC 1792 defines unspecified-network tables (tcpUnspecConnTable and udpUnspecTable). These tables omit the network address entirely, since the connection or listener accepts datagrams from any interface on the local node. The TCP unspecified table records only the state and local port, while the UDP unspecified table records only the local port.
sections.eli5: UDP is quicker but simpler than TCP. Instead of tracking a conversation, you just track which mailboxes are open. For mailboxes open to everyone, you do not even need to name which building they are in.

sections.title: Status and Security
sections.content:
RFC 1792 is an Experimental protocol and remains experimental. It was published in April 1995 and has not been obsoleted, updated, or advanced to higher standardization levels.

The RFC explicitly notes that security issues are not discussed in the document. MIB access control depends on the overall SNMP implementation. Network administrators should apply appropriate SNMP authentication and access controls to prevent unauthorized monitoring or manipulation of connection state.
sections.eli5: This is a test idea (experimental) from 1995. The security of what you can see and change depends on who you let use the monitoring tool.
